title: Universal fluctuations of first discoveries in competitive exploration
authors: Arthur Plaud, P. L. Krapivsky, S. Redner, Olivier Bénichou
abstract: Random exploration is usually quantified by how fast new space is found, from   the range of a single walker to the territory collectively covered by many   walkers. In competitive exploration, first arrival secures an exclusive resource, as when foragers compete for food items or agents capture distributed targets. It is then no longer enough to know which sites have been discovered: one must determine, for each discovered site, which searcher reached it first. We introduce the discovery   share $X_n$, the fraction of the first $n$ collective discoveries secured by   a tagged searcher. For two identical competitors, exchange symmetry fixes   $\langle X_n\rangle=1/2$, but the central question is whether this equal   split emerges in each long exploration history or only on average, \emph{i.e.} whether early   competitive advantages are erased or persist. Here we show that the answer is   controlled by the spectral dimension $d_s$, defined by the large-time decay of the probability that a single searcher is at   its starting point after $t$ steps, $p_0(t)\sim t^{-d_s/2}$.   Across ordinary diffusion, long-range superdiffusion and subdiffusion induced   by crowding or memory, $d_s$ separates persistent randomness in   recurrent exploration $(d_s<2)$, anomalously slow non-Gaussian concentration   for $2\le d_s<3$, and Gaussian concentration, logarithmically corrected at   $d_s=3$, for $d_s\ge3$. For $d_s\ge2$, we derive exact asymptotic   variances, including prefactors, and the discovery scale on which competitive   imbalances are erased. Two-point correlations of first-discovery labels identify the memory mechanism behind these regimes.   The same phase structure persists under changes in geometry, competitor   heterogeneity, number of competitors and memory, revealing a general fluctuation   theory of first-arrival inequalities.
summary: This work develops a general fluctuation theory for competitive exploration by analyzing the 'discovery share' of two searchers. The key finding links the persistence of early advantages to the spectral dimension ($d_s$) of the underlying random walk medium. A critical threshold at $d_s=2$ separates regimes where initial imbalances are erased from those where they persist.
main_problem: The paper investigates the universal fluctuations of the 'discovery share' ($X_n$)—the fraction of first discoveries secured by a tagged searcher—in competitive exploration.
main_result: The persistence of early competitive advantages depends critically on the spectral dimension ($d_s$): $d_s < 2$ implies persistent randomness, while $d_s \ge 2$ leads to concentration towards an equal split ($\langle X_n angle = 1/2$).
method: The analysis uses asymptotic methods based on the spectral dimension ($d_s$), which characterizes the large-time decay of single-walker return probabilities, leading to distinct scaling laws for the variance $	ext{Var}(X_n)$.
model_or_system: The model involves two identical searchers competitively exploring a landscape (random walk). The dynamics are analyzed across various media characterized by their spectral dimension ($d_s$), including ordinary diffusion, superdiffusion, and subdiffusion.
key_observables: Discovery Share ($X_n$), $	ext{Var}(X_n)$, two-point correlations of first-discovery labels ($	ext{Cov}(I_k, I_{k+\ell})$), and the spectral dimension ($d_s$).
important_parameters: Spectral Dimension ($d_s$); critical thresholds at $d_s=2$ (the self-averaging threshold) and $d_s=3$.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes Markovian searchers and initially focuses on two identical competitors, though the theory is shown to generalize.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the transition from persistent randomness ($d_s < 2$) to concentration towards $1/2$ ($d_s \ge 2$), showing how the spectral dimension governs this phase structure across different diffusion regimes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the definition of the discovery share and introduces the role of the spectral dimension. It then derives the asymptotic variance laws for various $d_s$ regimes, analyzes the memory mechanism via two-point correlations, and concludes by generalizing these fluctuation theories to other physical parameters.
why_interesting: While focused on random walks, the concept of 'memory' and how local advantages (first arrival) are erased or persist over time is highly relevant to non-equilibrium dynamics in complex systems, such as pattern formation or resource competition modeled using stochastic processes.
